questionText: Series: 64,81,100,121,... Which number NOT in series?
hints: Look at what kind of numbers are in the series. Each one comes from multiplying a number by itself.
64 is 8 × 8 and 81 is 9 × 9. Test each choice to see whether it is a number multiplied by itself.
Here is a similar one: the series 1, 4, 9, 16 holds square numbers. 49 belongs, because 7 × 7 = 49. 50 does not belong, because it falls between 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64.

stepByStep.text: The series is 8 × 8, 9 × 9, 10 × 10, 11 × 11. These are square numbers.
169 is 13 × 13, 225 is 15 × 15 and 289 is 17 × 17. They all belong.
13 × 13 = 169 and 14 × 14 = 196. No whole number multiplied by itself gives a number between these two.
176 lies between 169 and 196. So 176 is not in the series.

misconceptions.A: 169 is 13 × 13, so it is in the series. Look for the number that is not a number times itself.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 176 falls between 13 × 13 and 14 × 14, so it is not a square number.
misconceptions.C: 225 is 15 × 15, so it is in the series. Look for the number that is not a number times itself.
misconceptions.D: 289 is 17 × 17, so it is in the series. Look for the number that is not a number times itself.

questionText: Sum of series 1,3,5,7,...,27?
hints: These are the odd numbers in order, starting from 1. Sums of odd numbers starting from 1 make a special pattern.
Try small cases first, such as 1 + 3 and 1 + 3 + 5. Then count how many odd numbers there are from 1 to 27.
Here is a similar one: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 has 5 odd numbers and adds up to 25. That is 5 × 5. So the sum of the first 5 odd numbers is (5)².

stepByStep.text: Look at small cases. 1 + 3 = 4, which is 2 × 2. And 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, which is 3 × 3. The sum is always the count of odd numbers multiplied by itself.
Count the odd numbers from 1 to 27. Add 1 to 27 and halve it.
There are 14 odd numbers, so the sum is 14 × 14.

misconceptions.A: Count the odd numbers again. 27 is the 14th odd number, not the 13th.
misconceptions.B: Yes! There are 14 odd numbers from 1 to 27, so the sum is 14 × 14.
misconceptions.C: Count how many odd numbers there are: (27 + 1) ÷ 2. The sum is that count multiplied by itself.
misconceptions.D: The sum depends on how many odd numbers there are, not on how big the last one is. Count them: (27 + 1) ÷ 2.

questionText: 59th odd number prior to 726?
hints: You are counting backwards through the odd numbers. Odd numbers are 2 apart.
Find the first odd number just before 726. Then work out how many jumps of 2 take you from the 1st to the 59th.
Here is a similar one: the 10th odd number before 50. The 1st is 49. The 10th is 9 jumps of 2 further back. 9 × 2 = 18, and 49 − 18 = 31.

stepByStep.text: To go from the 1st to the 59th you make 58 jumps back, and each jump is 2.
So the 59th odd number before 726 is 609.

misconceptions.A: This is the 58th one. Count 725 as the 1st, then make 58 jumps of 2.
misconceptions.B: This is the 60th one. 725 is already the 1st, so you need 58 jumps, not 59.
misconceptions.C: 608 is an even number. The answer must be odd.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 725 is the 1st, and 58 jumps of 2 back from it reach 609.

questionText: Sum of 7th and 11th even numbers after greatest 2-digit prime?
hints: There are two jobs here. First find the greatest 2-digit prime number, then count the even numbers that come after it.

Here is a similar one: the 3rd and 5th even numbers after 13. The even numbers are 14, 16, 18, 20, 22. The 3rd is 18 and the 5th is 22. Their sum is 18 + 22 = 40.

stepByStep.text: 99 is 9 × 11 and 98 is even, so neither is prime. The greatest 2-digit prime is 97.
The 1st even number after 97 is 98. The 7th is 6 jumps of 2 further on.
228 is not among the numbers given. So the answer is None of these.

misconceptions.B: Count from 98 as the 1st even number. The 7th is 110 and the 11th is 118. Add those two.
misconceptions.C: This is far too big. The two numbers are 110 and 118. Add those two.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 110 + 118 = 228, and that number is not listed.

hints: Odd and even numbers take turns. The number just after an odd number is always even, and even numbers go up in 2s.
The 1st even number after W+9 is W+10. Now think how many jumps of 2 take you from the 1st even number to the 48th.
Similar example: N+5 is odd. The 1st even number after it is N+6. The 10th even number is 9 jumps of 2 further on: 9 × 2 = 18, and 6 + 18 = 24. So it is N+24.

From the 1st even number to the 48th there are 47 jumps of 2.
Add 94 to the 10. The 48th even number is W+104.

misconceptions.A: This comes from making 48 jumps of 2 from W+10. From the 1st even number to the 48th there are only 47 jumps.
misconceptions.B: Yes! W+10 is the 1st even number, and 47 more jumps of 2 land on W+104.
misconceptions.C: This is one jump short. W+10 is the 1st even number and 47 jumps of 2 follow it.
misconceptions.D: W+9 is odd, and this is 96 more than it, so it is odd too. The answer must be an even number.

questionText: (x+9) is 2-digit prime. Find 12th even number after it?
hints: A 2-digit prime number is always odd. So the number just after it is even, and even numbers go up in 2s.

Similar example: N+3 is an odd number. The 1st even number after it is N+4. The 6th even number is 5 jumps of 2 further: 5 × 2 = 10, and 4 + 10 = 14. So it is N+14.

misconceptions.D: One of the answers does match. Start from x+10 as the 1st even number and count on in 2s.

So the sum of the first 12 odd numbers is 12 times 12.
